title: How the Ancient Greeks Interpreted Their Dreams
author: Kristen French
text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementHistoryHow the Ancient Greeks Interpreted Their DreamsCertain concepts such as metaphor may derive from early dream interpretationKFBy Kristen French1:00 PM CDT on August 20, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleIn Homer’s The Odyssey, Penelope—Odysseus’ loyal wife—has several dreams. In one of these dreams, she watches 20 pet geese eating wheat far from the water. Suddenly, a massive mountain eagle swoops down from a mountain and breaks all of their necks, killing them. The dead geese lay scattered around the palace, and Penelope weeps in distress, but the eagle returns and speaks to her in a human voice: The geese represent her suitors, and the eagle stands in for Odysseus himself, who will kill all the suitors on his return, the bird tells her.Subscribe to skip adsFeatured VideoPowered By 10 Is This Exoplanet More Dense Than Steel?ShareNextStayThis dream interpretation is one of the earliest recorded in human history, and it bears certain striking features that are not only common across dream interpretation in ancient Greece—but that have shaped the study of meaning in language and text ever since. This is the argument that classicist Mirjam Kotwick makes in her new book The Ancient Interpretation of Dreams: a long line of Greek thinkers, including Homer, Aeschylus, Herodotus, Plato, and Aristotle, she writes, engaged in an intellectual practice of dream interpretation using a shared method—essentially reading by resemblance, or the logic of likeness—and this method continues to shape how we interpret figurative language today.I spoke with Kotwick about Penelope’s dream, the relationship between dream interpretation and magic, what Hippocrates thought the body could communicate through dreams, and what common modern concepts such as metaphor might have arisen from the ancient practice of dream interpretation.Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
